title: Chapter 2: Values and Variables: Giving Data a Name
video_title: Python Chapter 2: Values and Variables, with an AI Study Partner
summary: Learn the four basic Python types, store data in well-named variables, calculate with the seven arithmetic operators and predict every result before you run the code. You will also catch an AI assistant's confident mistake in an average calculation.

scenes.title: Why this matters
scenes.direction: Show the problem with the Chapter 1 receipt, then the fix in one line.

beats.narration: In Chapter 1, the cafe receipt typed each price twice: once in the item line, and once in the total. If the price of tea changes, you must find and change every copy. Miss one, and the receipt is wrong.

visual.heading: The problem: the same price, typed twice
body: In Chapter 1, the receipt typed each price in two places:
visual.pre:
print("Tea", "USD 3", sep=" ............. ")
...
print("Total: USD", 3 + 7)

Change the tea price?  You must change BOTH lines.

beats.narration: A variable solves this. A variable is a name that refers to a value. You store the price once, under a name such as tea price, and use that name everywhere.

visual.heading: The fix: give the value a name
body: A **variable** is a name that refers to a value.
Store the price once, then use the name everywhere:

scenes.title: The idea: values, types and assignment
scenes.direction: Table first, then the assignment diagram. Finish with the analogy and where it stops working.

beats.narration: A value is a single piece of data, such as 3, 3.5 or the word Tea. Every value has a type. The type tells Python what kind of data it is, and what you can do with it.

visual.heading: Every value has a type
rows: Numbers with a decimal point: prices
Yes or no facts: is a member

beats.narration: Python has four basic types. An int is a whole number. A float is a number with a decimal point. A string is text inside quotation marks. And a Boolean is either True or False.

visual.heading: Every value has a type
rows: Numbers with a decimal point: prices
Yes or no facts: is a member

beats.narration: Assignment connects a name to a value. You write the name, then the equals sign, then the value. Python works out the right side first. Then it connects the name on the left to the result.

visual.heading: Assignment connects a name to a value
body: Read `=` as **now refers to**, not as **is equal to**.
visual.pre:
name         value
 tea_price  =    3
     ^           |
     +-----------+
  Python works out the right side first,
  then connects the name on the left to it.

beats.narration: So read the equals sign as now refers to, not as is equal to. Think of a variable as a name label that you stick on a value. You can move the label to a new value at any time.

visual.heading: A variable is like a name label
items: You stick the label `tea_price` on the value `3`.
You can move the label to a new value at any time.
Where the comparison stops: two labels can point to the same value, and moving one label does not move the other.

visual.heading: Step 1: Create your first variables

beats.narration: Before you run it, predict the three lines of output.

beats.narration: Here is the output. Asha, then Tea costs 3, then Two teas cost 6. In the print on line 4, the name customer has no quotation marks. So Python prints its value, Asha, and not the word customer.

visual.heading: Step 1: Create your first variables

beats.narration: Good names make code easy to read. The Python style guide, called PEP 8, says: use lowercase letters, and join words with an underscore. A name can contain letters, digits and underscores, but it cannot start with a digit.

visual.heading: Naming rules (PEP 8)
items: Lowercase words joined by underscores: `tea_price`, not `TeaPrice` or `tp`.
Letters, digits and underscores only, and never a digit first.
Capital letters matter: `price` and `Price` are different names.
Do not use reserved words such as `True`, `None` or `class`.

beats.narration: Capital letters matter, so price with a small p and Price with a capital P are two different names. And do not use the words Python reserves for itself, such as True, None or class.

visual.heading: Naming rules (PEP 8)

scenes.title: Step 2: Check the type of a value
scenes.direction: Show the code with the output hidden, then reveal the output and point at each type.

beats.narration: Step 2. The type function tells you the type of any value. This program stores four values: a count of cups, a price, an item name and a yes or no fact. Then it prints each value with its type.

visual.heading: Step 2: Check the type of a value

beats.narration: Run it. The 2 is an int. The 3.5 is a float. Tea is a string, shown as s t r. And True is a bool.

visual.heading: Step 2: Check the type of a value

beats.narration: Python chose each type from the way you wrote the value. A decimal point makes a float, and quotation marks make a string. True and False need a capital first letter.

visual.heading: How Python chooses the type
items: A decimal point makes a `float`: `3.5`.
Quotation marks make a `str`: `"Tea"`.
`True` and `False` need a capital first letter.

scenes.title: Step 3: Calculate with operators
scenes.direction: Pause for the learner to predict all seven lines. After the reveal, use the table to explain the three surprising operators.

beats.narration: Step 3. An operator is a symbol that does a calculation. Seventeen biscuits are shared between five friends. This program uses all seven arithmetic operators.

visual.heading: Step 3: Calculate with operators

beats.narration: Pause the video and predict each line. Pay special attention to divide, floor divide and remainder.

visual.question: 17 biscuits, 5 friends. Predict all seven results.

beats.narration: Here are the results. Add gives 22, subtract gives 12, and multiply gives 85. Divide gives 3.4. Floor divide gives 3. Remainder gives 2. And power gives 25.

visual.heading: Step 3: Calculate with operators

beats.narration: Three operators often surprise beginners. A single slash is division. It gives the exact answer, 3.4, and the result is always a float. A double slash is floor division. It gives the whole part, so each friend gets 3 whole biscuits.

visual.heading: Three operators that surprise beginners
rows: The exact answer. It is always a `float`.

beats.narration: The percent sign gives the remainder, so 2 biscuits are left over. Finally, two stars raise a number to a power. So 5 to the power 2 is 5 times 5, which is 25.

visual.heading: Three operators that surprise beginners
rows: The exact answer. It is always a `float`.

scenes.title: Step 4: Change a variable
scenes.direction: Highlight each assignment line in turn so the learner can follow the value of points.

beats.narration: Step 4. A variable can get a new value. Here, points starts at 10. Line 4 says: points equals points plus 5.

visual.heading: Step 4: Change a variable

beats.narration: In mathematics, that line would be impossible. In Python, it means: take the current value of points, add 5, and give points the new value. Python works out the right side first.

visual.heading: Python works out the right side first

beats.narration: So the output shows Start 10, After a quiz 15, and After the bonus 30. Line 6 doubled the value of 15.

visual.heading: Step 4: Change a variable

scenes.title: Step 5: The order of operations
scenes.direction: Pause on the first two lines. After the reveal, explain line 4, then the inexact float on line 5 and round on line 6.

beats.narration: Step 5. Python follows the same order as mathematics. It calculates powers first. Then it multiplies and divides. Then it adds and subtracts. Brackets change the order.

visual.heading: Step 5: Know the order of operations
visual.note: Order: `**` first, then `*` `/` `//` `%`, then `+` `-`. Brackets go first of all.

beats.narration: Predict lines 2 and 3 before you look.
Line 2 multiplies first, so the result is 14. Line 3 adds first because of the brackets, so it gives 20. Line 4 divides first, and gives 8.0, a float, because division always gives a float.

visual.heading: Step 5: Know the order of operations

beats.narration: Line 5 is a surprise. Point 1 plus point 1 plus point 1 does not print exactly point 3. Computers store decimal numbers in binary, so some values, such as point 1, carry a tiny error. On line 6, the round function rounds the result to 2 decimal places, and you get point 3.

visual.heading: A float is not always exact

beats.narration: Here is the Write card. Paste your code, and ask the AI to predict the exact output line by line, without running or changing it. Then compare three things: your prediction, the AI's prediction and the real output.

visual.heading: Prompt card: predict first, then run
visual.label: Write
visual.prompt: Here is my Python code: <paste your code>. Do not change it and do not run it. Predict the exact output, line by line. For each line, explain in one sentence how Python calculated it.
visual.check: Write your own prediction first. Compare yours, the AI's and the real output.

beats.narration: And here is the Debug card. Give the AI the exact error message, and ask for the cause before the fix.

visual.heading: Prompt card: find the cause before the fix
visual.label: Debug
visual.prompt: I am a beginner. I ran this Python code: <paste the code>. I got this exact error: <paste the full error message>. First explain what the error means and which line causes it. Then show the smallest fix.
visual.check: Apply the fix, run the program, and confirm the explanation matches the error.

beats.narration: Now, the AI pair moment. Remember the puzzle from the start? The AI wrote this average, and predicted 90. It printed 203 point 3 3. Why?

visual.heading: AI pair moment: find the flaw

beats.narration: Use what you learned in step 5.

visual.question: Which operation does Python do first on line 5? Where do the brackets go?

beats.narration: The AI forgot the order of operations. Python divided only score 3 by 3, and then added the other two scores. Brackets around the sum fix the order, and the program prints 90.0.

visual.heading: The fix: brackets around the sum

beats.narration: A quick check would also catch this flaw. An average of three scores must be between the lowest and the highest score. A result of 203 is impossible. Code that runs is not always code that is correct.

visual.heading: The two-second check
items: An average must lie between the lowest and the highest value.
80, 90 and 100 cannot average 203.
Predict. Run. Compare.

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: One beat per mistake: the code and the real error side by side, then the fix in the narration.

beats.narration: Now, four common mistakes. Mistake 1 is a typing error in a variable name. Line 4 uses tea prise, spelled with an s. Python only knows the names you created, so it stops with a Name Error. It even suggests the right name.

visual.heading: Mistake 1: a typing error in a name

beats.narration: Mistake 2 is a number stored as text. With quotation marks, 3 is a string, not an int. Python will not add text and a number, so you get a Type Error. The fix is to remove the quotation marks.

visual.heading: Mistake 2: a number stored as text

beats.narration: Sometimes this mistake gives no error at all, which is worse. Multiplying the string 3 by 2 repeats the text, so you get 33 instead of 6. If a result looks strange, check the type.

visual.heading: The silent version of mistake 2

beats.narration: Mistake 3 is a name that starts with a digit. Python reads the 2 as the start of a number, and does not understand the letters after it. Start the name with a letter, such as second place.

visual.heading: Mistake 3: a name that starts with a digit

beats.narration: Mistake 4 puts the name and the value on the wrong sides. A literal is a value written directly in the code, such as 10, and it cannot get a new value. The name always goes on the left: points equals 10.

visual.heading: Mistake 4: the name and value on the wrong sides

beats.narration: The habit from Chapter 1 still works. Read the last line of an error first. It names the kind of error. Then look at the line number.

visual.heading: Read the last line first
rows: A misspelt name, or a name used before it exists
Text where a number was needed
A name starting with a digit
Put the name on the left
